_comment: Hand-curated landmark positions. Coordinates are the real thing, to about 100 m. `iso` is the country expected there; build-monuments.ts checks it against the baked outlines and complains when they disagree, which is how a wrong coordinate gets caught. `height` is the real structure in metres, for the info card only — the model's size comes from its tier in the monument contract. Leave a field out rather than guess it. `notes` is one sentence a landmark for the card that greets you there, keyed by id and written to be checked against a reference, not remembered.

notes.eiffel-tower: Built as the entrance arch of the 1889 World's Fair and meant to last twenty years; it was the tallest structure on Earth until 1930.
notes.arc-de-triomphe: Napoleon ordered it after Austerlitz in 1806; it took thirty years, and twelve avenues radiate from the star around it.
notes.mont-saint-michel: A granite islet crowned by a Benedictine abbey, in a bay where the tide is said to come in as fast as a galloping horse.
notes.colosseum: Opened in AD 80 with a hundred days of games; some 50,000 spectators sat under a canvas awning worked by sailors.
notes.leaning-tower-pisa: It began to lean in 1178, while it was still being built on soft ground; engineers took 40 cm off the lean between 1990 and 2001.
notes.st-peters-basilica: Michelangelo designed the dome of the largest church in the world, raised over the traditional tomb of Saint Peter.
notes.sagrada-familia: Gaudí gave it the last 43 years of his life and is buried in its crypt; begun in 1882, it is still being built.
notes.alhambra: The palace-fortress of the Nasrid sultans of Granada, its courts lined with carved stucco and cooled by water from the Sierra Nevada.
notes.guggenheim-bilbao: Frank Gehry's titanium-clad museum on the Nervión, whose success gave a name to the 'Bilbao effect'.
notes.big-ben: Big Ben is strictly the 13.7-tonne bell inside; the tower was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012 for the Queen's Diamond Jubilee.
notes.tower-bridge: A bascule bridge dressed as a Gothic castle; its two leaves still rise to let tall ships into the Pool of London.
notes.stonehenge: Raised in stages from about 3000 BC; its axis lines up with the midsummer sunrise and the midwinter sunset.
notes.brandenburg-gate: Berlin's neoclassical gate, crowned by the Quadriga, stood in the no man's land of the Wall until 1989.
notes.neuschwanstein: Ludwig II's fairy-tale castle, still unfinished when he died in 1886; it inspired Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle.
notes.atomium: Built for the 1958 World's Fair: an iron crystal cell magnified 165 billion times, its spheres joined by tubes and escalators.
notes.kinderdijk: Nineteen windmills built around 1740 to keep the polders of the Alblasserwaard drained, and most of them still turn.
notes.charles-bridge: Prague's stone bridge over the Vltava, begun under Charles IV in 1357 and lined with thirty Baroque statues.
notes.st-basils-cathedral: Ivan the Terrible built it on Red Square to mark the capture of Kazan; each of its chapels wears its own dome.
notes.parthenon: The temple of Athena on the Acropolis, finished in 438 BC; its columns swell and lean so that they look straight.
notes.hagia-sophia: For nearly a thousand years the largest cathedral in the world; its dome seems to float on a ring of forty windows.
notes.little-mermaid: Edvard Eriksen's bronze of Hans Christian Andersen's mermaid, only 1.25 metres tall, on a rock in Copenhagen harbour.
notes.hallgrimskirkja: Reykjavík's concrete church, its stepped tower modelled on the basalt columns that lava forms as it cools.
notes.borgund-stave-church: A wooden stave church from about 1180, its tiered roofs watched over by carved dragon heads.
notes.gergeti-trinity: A 14th-century church alone on a ridge at 2,170 metres, under the glaciers of Mount Kazbek.
notes.registan: Samarkand's great square, framed by three madrasas covered in blue tilework: the heart of the Timurid city.
notes.persepolis: The ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid kings, founded by Darius I around 518 BC and burned by Alexander in 330 BC.
notes.baalbek: Roman temples of Jupiter and Bacchus, raised on foundation stones that weigh up to 800 tonnes each.
notes.ziggurat-of-ur: A stepped temple mound built around 2100 BC for Nanna, the moon god of the Sumerian city of Ur.
notes.taj-mahal: The white marble tomb Shah Jahan built for Mumtaz Mahal; its stone shifts from pink to white to gold with the light.
notes.sigiriya: A palace on top of a rock 180 metres high, entered between the paws of a colossal stone lion, built by King Kashyapa in the 5th century.
notes.golden-temple: The holiest gurdwara of Sikhism, its gilded sanctum standing in a pool; its kitchen feeds tens of thousands every day.
notes.great-wall: Not one wall but many, built and rebuilt over two thousand years; its surveyed branches add up to 21,196 km.
notes.forbidden-city: The palace of the Ming and Qing emperors for five centuries: 980 buildings behind a moat and a ten-metre wall.
notes.terracotta-army: Some 8,000 life-size clay soldiers buried with China's first emperor around 210 BC, no two faces alike.
notes.potala-palace: The winter palace of the Dalai Lamas, thirteen storeys climbing the Red Hill above Lhasa at 3,700 metres.
notes.bagan: More than 2,000 Buddhist temples and pagodas still stand on the plain, of over 10,000 built between the 11th and 13th centuries.
notes.angkor-wat: The largest religious monument on Earth, built for Vishnu in the early 12th century; its five towers are lotus buds.
notes.petra: The Nabataeans carved their city into rose-red sandstone; the Treasury's façade is cut straight out of the cliff.
notes.burj-khalifa: The tallest building in the world since 2010, 828 metres to the tip of a spire visible from 95 km away.
notes.tokyo-tower: Modelled on the Eiffel Tower and 13 metres taller, painted white and international orange for air safety.
notes.mount-fuji: Japan's highest peak, a near-perfect cone of a volcano that last erupted in 1707.
notes.himeji-castle: The White Heron, Japan's finest surviving feudal castle, which came through the bombing of 1945 almost untouched.
notes.petronas-towers: The tallest twin towers in the world, joined by a skybridge at the 41st floor; each plan is an eight-pointed star.
notes.marina-bay-sands: Three hotel towers carrying a 340-metre SkyPark, with an infinity pool nearly 200 metres above the bay.
notes.borobudur: The largest Buddhist temple in the world, a 9th-century mountain of terraces holding 504 statues of the Buddha.
notes.taipei-101: Once the tallest building in the world, it rides out typhoons on a 660-tonne steel ball hung near its top.
notes.gyeongbokgung: The main palace of the Joseon kings, founded in 1395, burned in the invasions of 1592 and rebuilt in 1867.
notes.mount-everest: The highest point on Earth, 8,849 metres; Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary first stood on it in 1953.
notes.genghis-khan-statue: A 40-metre steel horseman on the steppe east of Ulaanbaatar; you can walk out onto the horse's head.
notes.hassan-ii-mosque: Built partly over the Atlantic in Casablanca, with a 210-metre minaret and a roof that slides open.
notes.pyramids-of-giza: The Great Pyramid of Khufu was the tallest thing people had built for almost 4,000 years, the last ancient wonder still standing.
notes.great-sphinx: A lion with a king's head, carved from the bedrock of the Giza plateau around 2500 BC, facing the sunrise.
notes.abu-simbel: Ramesses II's temples, cut into a cliff above the Nile; in the 1960s they were sawn apart and lifted 65 metres, out of Lake Nasser's way.
notes.djenne-mosque: The largest mud-brick building in the world; every year the whole town replasters it at the Crépissage festival.
notes.elmina-castle: Built by the Portuguese in 1482, the oldest European building south of the Sahara, later a hub of the Atlantic slave trade.
notes.lalibela: Eleven medieval churches carved downward into the living rock, joined by trenches and tunnels.
notes.kilimanjaro: Africa's highest mountain, a free-standing volcano of three cones whose summit glaciers are shrinking fast.
notes.victoria-falls: Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'the smoke that thunders': the Zambezi falls more than 100 metres along a curtain 1.7 km wide.
notes.avenue-of-the-baobabs: A dirt road lined with Grandidier's baobabs up to 800 years old, the last of a forest long since cleared.
notes.table-mountain: A flat-topped sandstone massif over Cape Town, often draped in the cloud the city calls its tablecloth.
notes.statue-of-liberty: A gift from France in 1886: copper skin on an iron frame designed by Gustave Eiffel, turned green within a few decades.
notes.empire-state: Built in 410 days during the Depression, it was the tallest building in the world for almost forty years.
notes.golden-gate-bridge: The longest suspension span in the world when it opened in 1937, painted a colour called International Orange.
notes.mount-rushmore: Four presidents, each face 18 metres tall, carved into the granite of the Black Hills between 1927 and 1941.
notes.space-needle: Built in 400 days for the 1962 World's Fair in Seattle, on a foundation deep enough to ride out earthquakes.
notes.cn-tower: Toronto's communications tower, the tallest free-standing structure in the world from 1976 until 2007.
notes.niagara-falls: Three falls on the border of Canada and the United States, together the most powerful waterfall in North America.
notes.chateau-frontenac: A railway hotel built as a château on the cliff above Quebec City, said to be the most photographed hotel in the world.
notes.citadelle-laferriere: The largest fortress in the Americas, built by Henri Christophe after Haiti's independence to hold off a French return.
notes.the-pitons: Two volcanic spires rising straight out of the Caribbean on the south-west coast of Saint Lucia.
notes.chichen-itza: At the equinoxes the afternoon sun draws a serpent of light down the northern stairs of El Castillo.
notes.teotihuacan: A city of perhaps 100,000 people around AD 450, laid out along the Avenue of the Dead below the Pyramid of the Sun.
notes.christ-the-redeemer: An Art Deco statue of reinforced concrete and soapstone on the 700-metre peak of Corcovado, arms open over Rio.
notes.angel-falls: The highest uninterrupted waterfall in the world, 979 metres off the lip of the tepui Auyán-tepui.
notes.las-lajas: A neo-Gothic basilica built across a river gorge in the south of Colombia, a few kilometres from Ecuador.
notes.machu-picchu: An Inca estate built around 1450 on a ridge above the Urubamba, missed by the Spanish and made famous in 1911.
notes.moai-rapa-nui: Nearly a thousand stone figures carved by the Rapa Nui; most stand with their backs to the sea, watching over the villages.
notes.perito-moreno: One of the few glaciers on Earth that is not retreating; its 70-metre front calves into Lago Argentino.
notes.sydney-opera-house: Jørn Utzon's shells took sixteen years to build, and their roofs carry more than a million glazed tiles.
notes.sydney-harbour-bridge: The 'Coathanger', opened in 1932, its steel arch rising 134 metres above the harbour.
notes.uluru: A sandstone monolith sacred to the Anangu, rising 348 metres from the desert and glowing red at sunset.
notes.moeraki-boulders: Spherical concretions up to two metres across, weathered out of the mudstone cliffs of the Otago coast.
notes.nan-madol: Nearly a hundred artificial islets of stacked basalt columns off Pohnpei, the seat of the Saudeleur dynasty.
notes.mount-yasur: One of the most accessible active volcanoes in the world, erupting several times an hour for at least 800 years.
notes.south-pole: The bottom of the world, on ice 2,700 metres thick; Amundsen's party reached it first, on 14 December 1911.
